clue.text: Crush baggage

blocks.note: first meaning: to beat or defeat heavily
second meaning: British slang for one's gear, clothes and belongings

explanation.walkthrough: As a noun the answer is British slang for personal gear or clothes; as a verb it means to hit hard or thrash.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb sense is to thrash an opponent; the noun sense is informal British for kit and possessions.

clue.text: Tenor, beloved Italian, touring America

indicators.note: a tour goes all around a place, so one word encircles the other

explanation.surface: A much-loved Italian singer goes on an American tour.
explanation.definitionFit: Enrico Caruso was the celebrated Italian operatic tenor of the early twentieth century.

clue.text: Heads of operations regularly talk vacantly about new media?

indicators.note: heads are tops, so only the first letter of each word is kept
about means surrounding, so the talk wraps around the next item

blocks.note: first letters of operations and regularly
to gas is to chatter idly

explanation.surface: An operations chief keeps prattling on about the new media.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' looks like an alternate-letter signal, but it is just a second word to take the head of.
explanation.definitionFit: Newspapers and journals are organs, the means through which views are published, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Son cuddling daughter appeared before artist: pictures come from this

indicators.note: to cuddle is to hold someone close in one's arms, enclosing them

explanation.surface: A family portrait: a boy hugging his sister, posed ahead of the painter.
explanation.walkthrough: RA, a Royal Academician, is the stock crossword artist.
explanation.definitionFit: A small video recorder worn on a police officer's uniform produces footage, the pictures in question.

clue.text: One's known for charging in, interrupting character from Greece

indicators.note: something that interrupts breaks into the middle of something else

blocks.note: a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: A notorious gatecrasher barges in on a Greek fellow's conversation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'charging in' reads as a phrase, but 'in' is the wordplay piece.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhinoceros is famous for lowering its horn and stampeding at threats.

clue.text: Vehicular problem presented by bonk in truck

blocks.note: to bonk or to bed someone is to have sex with them

explanation.surface: A cheeky tale of car trouble arising from a romp in the back of a lorry.
explanation.walkthrough: Bonk is British slang for having sex, as is the verb bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A lorry with an open, level loading platform and no sides is called by this name.

clue.text: Confront keeping church in whack? Not a hope

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it within
in places the religious piece within the next word

blocks.note: to tan someone's hide is to beat them

explanation.surface: Facing a church over corporal punishment? No chance.
explanation.walkthrough: To tan someone's hide is an old phrase for beating them, so 'whack' is a verb here, not slang for crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is sarcastic: saying something has a large chance means there is no likelihood at all.

clue.text: Welsh parliamentarian has way of working material for attack

blocks.note: Assembly Member, of the Welsh Assembly

explanation.surface: A Welsh politician has a method for gathering material to attack rivals.
explanation.walkthrough: AM was the title of a member of the Welsh Assembly, now the Senedd.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for ammunition, it also means figurative fodder for an argument.

clue.text: Tie up Bill, uplifted about bit of hanky-panky in loo

indicators.note: in a down entry, lifting up makes the letters read from the bottom
a bit of a word here is its first letter
about means going around the following letter

blocks.note: to moor a boat is to tie it up

explanation.surface: Something saucy happens in the lavatory involving restraints.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uplifted' reverses both the tie-up word and the bill together, since this is a down answer read from the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: Loo is British informal for toilet, and a toilet room is commonly called this, especially in America.

clue.text: Deny record target involving head of livestock

indicators.note: involving means taking something into the middle
the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A farmer rejects claims about a sales target for cattle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involving' acts on the record and target joined together: the livestock letter sits at their join.
explanation.definitionFit: To disclaim is to renounce or refuse to acknowledge responsibility, a formal way to deny.

clue.text: Falsify documents, making no allowances

blocks.note: to rig is to fix or falsify

explanation.surface: Someone forging papers in a strict, unbending way.
explanation.definitionFit: A strict, inflexible person or rule is one that refuses any leeway or exceptions.

clue.text: Hints at coming in early enough, before start of session

indicators.note: one word arriving inside another means it is placed within it
the start of a word is its opening letter only

explanation.surface: Someone suggests arriving punctually, ahead of a meeting's start.
explanation.walkthrough: AT goes inside IN TIME, between M and E, then S follows: INTIMATES. 'Hints at' looks like the definition, but 'at' belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to intimate is to suggest or imply something indirectly, so the third-person form matches the verb hints.

clue.text: You might ask for a hand using this?

definitions.text: You might ask for a hand using this?

blocks.clueFragment: You might ask for a hand

blocks.note: setter's reading: 'hand' for a whole worker is the figure of speech where a part stands for the whole

explanation.walkthrough: Asking for 'a hand' when you want a whole person to help is the classic example of a part standing for the whole.
explanation.definitionFit: The term names a figure of speech in which a part stands for the whole, as hands means workers.

clue.text: Speaking about planetary motion no little amount

indicators.note: 'no' says the following item is to be taken away entirely

blocks.note: relating to the path of a planet
a bit is a small amount

explanation.surface: A lecture on the motion of planets that skimps nowhere.
explanation.walkthrough: ORBITAL minus BIT leaves ORAL. 'about' is part of the wordplay, not a link: things about planetary motion are orbital.
explanation.definitionFit: An oral exam or account is a spoken one, so the adjective fits 'speaking' used attributively.

clue.text: Subsidiary line subsequently brought in fuel

indicators.note: something brought in is taken inside the next word

explanation.surface: A branch railway line later carries a fuel supply.
explanation.definitionFit: Collateral can mean secondary or additional, as in collateral damage, matching subsidiary.

clue.text: The writer's advisor accepting second idea, initially as a reminder of impermanence

indicators.note: to accept is to take in, so the advisor holds the next piece inside
initially points to the very first letter of the word before it

blocks.note: the writer is me, and 'the writer's' = 'the writer is'
a mo is a moment, a second

explanation.surface: An author's counsellor takes on board a fresh thought.
explanation.walkthrough: A mo is British informal for a moment, as in 'half a mo'. 'The writer's' reads as 'the writer is', giving the pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase, 'remember you must die', names an object such as a skull kept to recall that life is short.

clue.text: Low source of luminance in darkness? Yes and no

definitions.text: Low source of luminance in darkness? Yes and no

blocks.clueFragment: Low source of luminance in darkness?
blocks.note: surface: a dim lamp at night
setter's reading: it lights the night faintly, yet the body it comes from only reflects the sun, so it is not truly a source

explanation.walkthrough: The light we see at night from our satellite is weak, but 'yes and no' because it is borrowed sunlight, not its own.
explanation.definitionFit: The glow from Earth's satellite is a faint night illumination, though reflected rather than generated.

clue.text: School's latest intention: old writer to turn up, covering two terms

indicators.note: the latest letter of a word is its final one
turning up in a down answer flips the order so it reads upward

explanation.surface: A school plans for an elderly author to visit over two terms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terms' suggests school terms, but they are algebraic terms.
explanation.definitionFit: In algebra a binomial is an expression of exactly two terms, such as x + y.

clue.text: Soprano - safe bet to retain focus for composer

indicators.note: to retain is to hold on to, keeping something within

explanation.surface: A singer who backs a sure thing stays the centre of attention for a composer.
explanation.walkthrough: A cert is British slang for a dead certainty, often in horse racing.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Schubert was the Austrian composer of lieder and symphonies.

clue.text: Popular study probing pink shade of body? Definitely not

indicators.note: something that probes pushes into the middle of something else

blocks.note: to pore over is to study closely

explanation.surface: A trendy examination of skin tone, followed by a firm denial.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a jokey paraphrase: 'of body? Definitely not' describes the opposite of bodily.
explanation.definitionFit: Something incorporeal has no physical form, the reverse of bodily.

clue.text: Not nearby? About to keep volume raised

indicators.note: raised in a down entry means read upward, from bottom to top
to keep something is to hold it inside

explanation.surface: A query about holding the sound level high far away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'volume' suggests loudness, but it is a book.
explanation.definitionFit: A remote place is far away, the opposite of near at hand.

clue.text: I don't know: large car missing latest couple of points

indicators.note: missing its latest means the final letter has gone

explanation.surface: A puzzled shrug about why a big car has lost recent race points.
explanation.definitionFit: This diacritic is two dots placed over a vowel, as in German, hence a pair of points.

clue.text: Sets up orchestra partly for backing musical work

indicators.note: only part of the run of words is used, sitting across their boundary
backing means moving backwards, so the letters read in the other direction

blocks.note: found across the end of sets, all of up and the start of orchestra

explanation.surface: An orchestra rehearses accompaniment for a composition.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for work, the term labels a numbered composition in a composer's catalogue.

clue.text: Fielders run amongst players to take advantage of other movement

indicators.note: a thing amongst others is surrounded by them

blocks.note: slips are close catching positions in cricket
R for run in cricket scoring

explanation.surface: Cricket fielders dash between team-mates to exploit a moment of play.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the slips are fielders standing beside the wicketkeeper. R goes inside TEAM.
explanation.definitionFit: To slipstream is to ride in the low-pressure wake behind a moving vehicle, gaining from its motion.

clue.text: I want you to cut petitions

indicators.note: cutting trims off the end of the phrase's word

explanation.surface: Someone asking another to shorten their appeals.
explanation.walkthrough: PLEASE loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A plea is an earnest request or appeal, so the plural matches petitions.

clue.text: Fruit alone displays different core

indicators.note: a different core means the middle letters are rearranged while the ends stay put

explanation.surface: A single piece of fruit shows a strange centre.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle two letters of SOLE swap places.
explanation.definitionFit: The sloe is the small bitter blue-black fruit of the blackthorn, used in sloe gin.

clue.text: Goolie due for treatment? One's fixed

indicators.note: treatment works the material over, so these letters are processed into a new order

explanation.surface: A man's testicle needs medical attention and gets mended.
explanation.walkthrough: Goolie is British slang for a testicle; 'fixed' looks surgical but means rigidly held in belief.
explanation.definitionFit: A dogmatic adherent of a doctrine holds views that are fixed and unbending.

clue.text: Old Judge in broadcast knocked back wine

indicators.note: knocked back means pushed backwards, so the word is read right to left
in says the earlier pieces sit inside the later word

explanation.surface: An elderly judge on the radio admits to downing some wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocked back' suggests drinking, fitting the wine, but it reverses AIR to RIA, which then holds OJ.
explanation.definitionFit: Rioja is a Spanish red or white from the region of that name.

clue.text: I will avoid literary theft, being most flexible

indicators.note: what avoids something keeps away from it, so that letter is left out

blocks.note: lit is the abbreviation for literary

explanation.surface: A writer vows never to plagiarise, as the most adaptable course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Literary theft' wants to mean plagiarism, but the two words work separately as an abbreviation and a robbery.
explanation.definitionFit: Lithe means supple and bending easily, so the superlative is the most supple.

clue.text: Significant article about fiction is set in stone

indicators.note: about means going around, so the article wraps the next word
set in puts the built word inside the last one

blocks.note: st is the abbreviation for stone, an imperial weight

explanation.surface: A notable newspaper piece on myths, carved into a monument.
explanation.walkthrough: Stone is an imperial weight of 14 pounds, still used in Britain for body weight; the article wraps the fiction first.
explanation.definitionFit: A salient point is one that stands out as most important or noticeable.
